questions.prompt: What makes a set of controls into a real security program?

options.text: It is governed, prioritized, and measured — layered so no single failure is fatal
It uses the most expensive tools available
It is completed once and never revisited

questions.explanation: A program is the governed, prioritized, measured whole — defense in depth across functions — not a pile of disconnected tools.

questions.prompt: Order the six NIST CSF 2.0 functions.
questions.explanation: CSF 2.0's functions are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover, with Govern steering the rest.

questions.prompt: Match each control to the NIST CSF function it belongs to.
questions.explanation: Controls map to functions: knowing your estate (Identify), preventing harm (Protect), seeing attacks (Detect), and restoring/learning (Recover).

questions.prompt: Which are highest-leverage 'do first' basics? Select all that apply.

options.text: MFA everywhere, especially email and admin
Buying advanced tools before deploying MFA or backups

questions.explanation: MFA, patching, backups (and least privilege, inventory, logging) give the most risk reduction per effort; advanced tools on a weak foundation don't.

questions.prompt: The average time it takes to notice an attack is the mean time to ____ (MTTD).
questions.explanation: MTTD (mean time to detect) and MTTR (mean time to respond/recover) are outcome metrics that reflect how much damage an incident causes.

questions.prompt: Why is buying advanced security tools before the basics a mistake?

options.text: Attackers walk in through simple gaps like no MFA or unpatched services that fancy tools can't compensate for
Basics are more expensive than advanced tools
It is required by every compliance framework

questions.explanation: Without fundamentals like MFA, patching, and backups, attackers exploit simple, common weaknesses; prioritize the highest-leverage basics first.
